page.name: Two-factor authentication
page.h1: Two-factor authentication codes, sent in time
page.metaDescription: Login-challenge codes delivered with per-number pacing and a written record, without conflating them with promotional traffic.
page.lede: A 2FA message is triggered by a login attempt, is time-critical, and — when it arrives unexpectedly — is the earliest signal your customer gets that someone else has their password. Send it fast, word it as a warning, and keep the record.

sections.h: What a good code message contains
bullets: The code, formatted so it is easy to transcribe
A plain statement of what triggered it
An explicit “if this was not you” instruction
Nothing else — no links to anything other than your own domain

sections.h: The unexpected code is doing its job
p: If a message arrives that the customer did not request, it is the earliest signal available that someone else has their password. Wording it as a warning rather than a nuisance is what turns the message into a security control instead of a support ticket.

sections.h: Absorb the login spike instead of dropping it
p: Login traffic is spiky and unpredictable. On the SMS channel, pacing is applied per sender number and routing can move traffic to another connected account, so a spike is absorbed as a delay rather than a wave of failures.
bullets: Per-number pacing instead of one shared quota
Every send logged, so an incident can be reconstructed

faq.q: Can a 2FA code be suppressed by an opt-out?
faq.a: No. Suppression applies to promotional traffic; a login challenge is transactional and is not filtered by the same rule.

faq.q: Should 2FA and marketing go out from the same number?
faq.a: That is a sender-identity decision. Keeping security traffic on a number that only sends security traffic makes an unexpected message easier for the customer to interpret.
Each send is logged with its status, and delivery receipts are recorded wherever the provider reports them, so an incident review works from a record rather than a recollection.
